claims.text: Premelting and melting behavior is governed by local chemical segregation.
Differences in constituent surface energies and atomic diffusivities drive local chemical segregation.
Local chemical segregation produces nanoscale regions of short-range order.
Segregated nanoscale regions have altered thermodynamic stability.
Segregated regions act as premelting sites.
Premelting sites reduce the energy barrier for melting onset.
Local segregation lowers the effective melting onset relative to a chemically homogeneous solid solution.
The initially synthesized Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are chemically homogeneous solid solutions.
Post-synthesis annealing will reduce local chemical fluctuations and pre-existing surface segregation.
Relevant compositional fluctuations include elemental clusters or segregated regions, particularly at nanoparticle surfaces.
As-synthesized nanoparticles will begin premelting at a lower temperature than annealed, chemically homogenized nanoparticles.
Premelting will first be observable as localized surface disorder followed by melting.
Segregation-driven premelting will produce distinct lower-temperature melting signals in thermal analysis or in situ imaging.
The proposed mechanism applies in a nanoparticle size regime where surface effects dominate.
The mechanism may cease to apply to larger particles or bulk materials because surface segregation is less influential there.
Heating rate may affect the relationship between kinetic effects and equilibrium segregation.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as chemically homogeneous, while the intervention and prediction assume that the as-synthesized particles contain pre-existing local fluctuations, elemental clusters, or surface segregation. The distinction between global compositional homogeneity and local segregation is not explicitly made.
